description: Hi, we’re CosmicPhantoms. We’re a small team working remotely on the Martian Map challenge. We both love space, and Mars especially, and we like making science feel less intimidating and more fun to explore. We’re just getting started, so your ideas can shape where this goes. We’re looking for people into data analysis, data visualization, planetary science or UI design, but curious beginners are welcome. We’ll keep things friendly, talk often and share the work fairly. Come build with us.
summary: The team created Drive the Real Mars, a free 3D browser game that lets students, educators and anyone curious about space drive NASA's Mars rovers over the same ground they explored. Players choose Perseverance, Curiosity or Spirit and play through 12 levels and 86 stops, each one a place the rover actually visited. The terrain is built from HiRISE elevation models and every stop comes from NASA rover records, turning Mars map data into a world players can explore for themselves. They plan routes on the orbital map, avoid slopes that could tip the rover, manage the battery, and drill or inspect rocks to see the photos the rover took at that exact spot. Ada, the mission controller, guides them with quick questions and side missions along the way. This directly addresses the challenge of making Martian map data understandable and engaging. Instead of viewing Mars only through pictures and flat maps, players experience the true distances, slopes and decisions rover drivers face. It promotes active learning, curiosity and scientific thinking, and it needs no account and runs on a laptop or phone, so anyone can start exploring Mars right away.
details:
• What does it do, and how does it work as the player sits down to drive the Mars rover?

It recreates three Mars rover missions as drives you can play, with Perseverance in Jezero crater, Curiosity in Gale crater and Spirit in Gusev crater. Across 12 levels and 86 stops, you retrace each rover's route through the places it explored, seeing the terrain from the ground up the way the rover did. Each level starts on the orbital map, where you plan your route around steep slopes and rough ground by setting waypoints. Then you drive in 3D, switching between the outside view and the rover's own view, with a mini-map showing where you are. Slopes slow the rover, tilting too far tips it over, and driving drains the battery, so you hold Recharge when it runs low. When you reach a stop, you park inside the ring and drill or inspect the rock. A card then shows the photos the rover took at that spot, and compares the sol you arrived with the sol the rover was actually there. Ada, your mission controller, guides the story, asks a quick question at each stop and sets side missions when the rover glitches. Collecting samples unlocks slope and elevation layers on the map, and each level ends with a result card you can share.

• What benefits does it have for the students, teachers and other learners who enjoy it?

It turns NASA's Mars map data into something you can explore hands-on rather than just look at. You learn how rover drivers think about slopes, battery and distance by doing it yourself. It's free, needs no account or install, and runs in a browser on a laptop or phone.

• What is the intended impact of this project on the classrooms and minds it will reach?

Mars has been mapped in incredible detail, yet most people only see it as pictures or flat maps. We want students and anyone curious to feel the true scale of these missions and come away knowing where each rover went and what it found.

• What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop the game?

We built the game with JavaScript, HTML and CSS, using three.js for 3D, and used Python with NumPy, Pillow, SciPy and tifffile to process NASA data. The data comes from HiRISE elevation models, USGS mosaics, NASA/JPL traverse maps and raw rover images, and the MER Analyst's Notebook. We used Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini for coding help, research and editing. The music is generated live in the browser, Vercel hosts the game and no special hardware is needed.

• How is your project creative, and what makes it stand out from the usual way to learn?

Instead of reading about a rover's journey, you drive it yourself, stop by stop, on terrain built from NASA's own elevation data. The story with Ada turns mission data into a campaign, with a mission controller guiding you, quick questions at each stop and side missions when the rover glitches, so learning happens along the way rather than in a separate quiz. Each stop rewards you with the rover's own photos from that day and shows how your timing compares with the real mission. Unlocking slope and elevation layers as you collect samples mirrors how rover teams use different maps to plan drives. Even the music is generated live in the browser. Together, it turns open science data into an experience that feels like a mission rather than a lesson.

• What factors did the team consider when planning, designing, building and testing it?

Accuracy came first. Terrain, coordinates and stops come from NASA data, and anything approximated is listed openly in the game's data panel, including surface colours, fine detail under 1 m, the sky and dust, power use while driving and the simplified rover model. Spirit's stops may be off by some tens of metres, and the AI-generated rover drawings are labelled as such. We also considered access, so it runs on laptops and phones with large touch controls, no sign-up and nothing to install. For learning, each stop has one quick question with the answer explained, and there are no points or scores to distract from exploring. We kept the controls simple and added a help screen so first-time players can start quickly. Finally, we tested the game on both laptop and phone layouts to make sure it plays smoothly on either.
